sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content:
August 2026 delivered a broadly constructive month for global equities, with the MSCI World advancing **+2.6%** and emerging markets outperforming at **+3.4%**. The S&P 500 gained **+2.7%** to **7,686.14** while the Nasdaq Composite surged **+4.0%** to **26,370.89** — the latter its best August since 2021 — as a powerful AI earnings cycle restored conviction in megacap technology. The developed-market MSCI EAFE advanced **+2.0%**, with European and select Asian benchmarks participating in the risk-on tone, though performance varied materially by region.

The month's gains were anchored in two primary catalysts: a resurgent AI capital-expenditure cycle, headlined by Nvidia's blockbuster fiscal Q2 results showing **+106%** revenue growth, and a geopolitically-driven energy complex rally that lifted commodity-linked markets across Europe. Basic resources stocks surged **+10.5%** in euro terms, supporting European indices, while semiconductor supply chains in Taiwan (**+6.44%**) and Korea (**+5.92%**) led emerging markets higher. Japan underperformed due to BOJ-driven carry trade disruption and yen appreciation.

The final trading week saw volatility re-enter the picture as Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh delivered a notably hawkish speech at Jackson Hole on August 28, signalling potential rate hikes and partially reversing the month's dollar weakness. Despite the end-of-month turbulence, global equity breadth remained constructive, with the majority of sectors and geographies posting positive monthly returns and the S&P 500 extending its year-to-date gain to **+13.1%**.

sections.title: Your Must-Know Market Themes
sections.content: Four key themes that shaped markets this month:
themes: Iran Geopolitical Shock & Oil Supply Squeeze -- The dominant macro force in August was the dramatic escalation of US-Iran tensions. Secondary sanctions from the US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control targeted Iranian oil exports and shipping intermediaries, while attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz directly constrained Middle East supply arteries. Brent crude rallied from approximately **$83/bbl** at the start of August to a peak of **$94.12/bbl** on August 24, before settling near **$90/bbl** (approx., verify before merging) at month-end — a gain of roughly **+9%** for the month. The Energy sector was the undisputed market beneficiary, advancing **+7.4%** in August after a **+12%** gain in July, leading all S&P 500 sectors for a second consecutive month. Surging diesel crack spreads — outpacing the headline crude benchmark move — pointed to tighter refined-product supply than futures alone conveyed, complicating the global inflation outlook and keeping fiscal and monetary risk premia elevated across fixed income markets.

Gold's Historic Monthly Surge -- August 2026 will be remembered as one of gold's most spectacular months on record, with the metal rallying approximately **+13%** to close at **$4,563/oz**, the third-highest monthly return for the metal in a quarter-century. The rally was multifactorial: a weakening US dollar in the first three weeks (the DXY fell to an intraday low of **98.55** on August 24), escalating Middle East geopolitical risk, a decisive technical breakout above the 200-day moving average, and deepening concern about US fiscal sustainability following mid-month CBO deficit projections. The debasement narrative — fuelled by sustained White House pressure on Fed independence and a record Treasury issuance calendar — attracted fresh institutional and sovereign allocations to bullion. Copper similarly hit a COMEX intraday record high of **$6.77/lb** on August 7, underpinned by AI-driven electrification demand and constrained mine supply from global labor disputes. A partial reversal in both metals occurred in the final two trading sessions after Chair Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole address strengthened the dollar, but the bulk of August's extraordinary advance proved durable.

Fed Chair Warsh's Hawkish Jackson Hole Address -- The most consequential single event of the month was Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh's August 28 keynote at the Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium, where he delivered a sharper-than-expected inflation warning and signalled that rates may need to move higher if disinflation progress stalls. Warsh unambiguously recommitted to the Fed's **2%** PCE inflation target, characterising current policy as insufficiently restrictive given persistent energy-driven inflation and resilient aggregate demand. Markets repriced immediately: the 2-year Treasury yield spiked **+12bps** to **4.34%** on the day, fed funds futures shifted to price a **60%** probability of a September rate hike (from roughly **56%** beforehand), and equities pared monthly gains. The speech placed Warsh in direct public tension with the White House's sustained demands for lower borrowing costs, elevating the political uncertainty premium around Fed independence and putting US monetary policy at the centre of the autumn macro debate. This friction — between a hawkish new Fed chair, an interventionist executive branch, and a bond market already digesting record fiscal supply — represents the defining macro risk for global capital markets as markets enter Q4.

AI Mega-Cycle Powers Nasdaq Leadership -- The singular force differentiating Nasdaq performance from broader benchmarks in August was a resurgent AI earnings super-cycle. Nvidia's fiscal Q2 results showed revenue growth of **+106%** year-over-year with Q3 guidance materially above consensus, confirming that hyperscaler AI infrastructure capital expenditure remains on an uninterrupted upward trajectory. AI-adjacent semiconductor names recovered sharply from July's consolidation, driving the Nasdaq Composite to a **+4.0%** gain versus the S&P 500's **+2.7%** advance. The global semiconductor supply chain re-rated in sympathy: Taiwan surged **+6.44%** and Korea gained **+5.92%** for the month, both benefiting from upward earnings revisions across the AI and high-bandwidth memory supply chain. Technology and Communication Services led all S&P 500 sectors aside from Energy, and sell-side analysts broadly raised 2026-2027 earnings estimates for AI-exposed names following the Nvidia print, reinforcing the sector's durable structural growth premium and extending the AI investment cycle into what many strategists are now calling its second, infrastructure-build phase.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
The S&P 500 gained **+2.7%** in August to close at **7,686.14**, extending its year-to-date advance to **+13.1%**, while the Nasdaq Composite surged **+4.0%** to **26,370.89** — its best August since 2021. The Dow Jones Industrial Average posted a more modest gain of approximately **+1%** to close near **53,185.90**, reflecting its lower technology weighting relative to the Nasdaq-heavy benchmarks. August represented a clean momentum reversal from July, when tech-heavy indices had given back ground.

Sectorally, Energy led for the second consecutive month, gaining **+7.4%** as Iran-related supply constraints propelled Brent crude sharply higher. Technology and Communication Services followed closely, buoyed by Nvidia's **+106%** Q2 revenue growth and broad AI infrastructure earnings strength that drew investors back into the megacap growth trade. Consumer Discretionary and Financials also contributed positively. Consumer Staples lagged as margin compression and demand softness weighed on the sector. Mid-August saw the Dow post back-to-back weekly losses as an inflation data print temporarily elevated rate hike expectations, pressuring rate-sensitive sectors before the index recovered.

The month's final session saw the S&P 500 slip as Warsh's Jackson Hole message raised September rate hike probabilities to **60%**, but the index still printed a solid monthly close. With the S&P 500 at **+13.1%** year-to-date, market participants entered September balanced between AI-cycle enthusiasm and a newly reactivated monetary policy uncertainty that had been largely dormant through the summer.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equities delivered a solid month broadly in line with global risk appetite. Germany's DAX 40 hit a record closing high of **26,001.31** during August, driven by renewed optimism around US-Iran diplomatic engagement prospects, strong industrial earnings, and the global commodity tailwind. The MSCI EAFE gained **+2.0%** for the month, with Basic Resources the standout sector at **+10.5%** in euro terms, supported by higher copper and gold prices, a weaker US dollar through mid-month, and robust earnings from European mining majors including Rio Tinto and Glencore.

The FTSE 100 advanced during August (end-of-month level approx., verify before merging), with the index's sizeable energy sector exposure providing a direct tailwind from the Brent crude rally. Early-August volatility — consistent with the global BOJ-carry-unwind shock — created a buying opportunity in UK equities that was substantially recovered by mid-month, with the FTSE benefiting from energy and materials strength. The CAC 40 similarly trended higher, led by luxury goods and materials, with the weaker dollar boosting European export competitiveness through most of the month before the Warsh-driven dollar reversal in the final days.

European sovereign bond yields rose in tandem with Treasuries, reflecting shared concerns about fiscal sustainability and energy-driven inflation stickiness. The ECB maintained a cautious, data-dependent stance in public communications ahead of its September meeting. The simultaneous advance in both yields and equities signals that European markets are pricing an earnings re-acceleration rather than a cyclical downturn — a constructive but fragile equilibrium that remains highly sensitive to energy price dynamics and central bank forward guidance.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Asia-Pacific equity markets delivered a sharply bifurcated performance in August, divided along monetary policy and AI supply chain exposure. Japanese equities were the notable regional underperformer: the Nikkei 225 declined toward the **64,011** area during the month (approx., verify before merging), pressured by the Bank of Japan's continued policy normalisation. BOJ board members reiterated intentions to raise rates as underlying inflation approaches the **2%** target, triggering yen carry trade unwinds, sharp yen appreciation, and meaningful headwinds for Japan's export-exposed corporate sector — a dynamic that echoed the August 2024 carry unwind playbook.

North Asian technology markets staged a strong recovery. Taiwan's benchmark surged **+6.44%** and the Korean KOSPI gained **+5.92%** for the month, driven by Nvidia's earnings-cycle confirmation and fresh AI capital-expenditure demand visibility across the semiconductor and HBM memory supply chains. The Hang Seng Index ended the month near the **26,009** level (approx., verify before merging) as geopolitical caution around cross-strait risk and ongoing China property sector structural concerns limited upside despite the global commodity tailwind. The Shanghai Composite hovered near **3,905** (approx., verify before merging), where domestic stimulus measures provided a floor but failed to catalyse a breakout amid subdued consumer demand data.

The APAC narrative for August reflects a region increasingly divided by the pace of BOJ normalisation, AI supply chain positioning, and China's growth trajectory. BOJ policy is now widely viewed as the single most consequential variable for intra-APAC equity allocation, as the erosion of the yen carry premium continues to narrow the valuation arbitrage that had underpinned both Japanese equity hedges and broader EM positioning.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The US dollar followed a distinctive two-phase arc in August: weakening materially through the first three weeks before a sharp Warsh-driven reversal. The DXY opened the month near **99.78**, fell to an intraday low of **98.55** on August 24, then recovered to close at **100.23** — a net **+0.5%** gain for the month despite the volatile round-trip. The dominant first-half dollar narrative centred on debasement: rising gold prices, geopolitical risk premia, CBO deficit projections, and White House pressure on Fed independence collectively undermined the greenback before Warsh's intervention at Jackson Hole reversed the trend.

EUR/USD hovered in the mid-**1.15–1.16** range through most of August (approx., verify before merging), supported by a constructive European risk environment and relatively steady ECB rhetoric. GBP/USD traded in a range of approximately **1.32–1.39** (approx., verify before merging), settling near the **1.36** area at month-end as the Bank of England offered no new forward guidance to drive directional conviction. USD/JPY was the most volatile of the G10 major pairs, oscillating between **152** and **164** during the month as BOJ rate hike signalling accelerated yen carry unwinds that had previously sustained the pair at elevated levels.

The overarching FX theme was the tentative erosion of dollar exceptionalism, temporarily arrested by Warsh's hawkish pivot. G10 FX volatility registered near its lowest levels since 2022 during the month's midsection — a complacency that Warsh's Jackson Hole address shattered in the final trading sessions. The medium-term structural dollar outlook remains bearish in the consensus view, with speculative positioning across major FX options markets persistently net-short US dollars.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
August 2026 was a landmark month for commodities, headlined by gold's historic **+13%** advance to close at **$4,563/oz** — its strongest monthly return in over 25 years. The rally was simultaneously a geopolitical hedge, a dollar debasement play, and a momentum-driven technical breakout above the 200-day moving average, with fresh sovereign and institutional allocations into bullion accelerating the move. Copper matched the bullish tone, setting a COMEX intraday record at **$6.77/lb** on August 7 before averaging approximately **$6.59/lb** for the month, underpinned by AI electrification infrastructure demand and constrained mine supply from global labor disputes.

Energy markets provided the month's other defining commodity narrative. Brent crude rallied from roughly **$83/bbl** at month-open to a peak of **$94.12/bbl** on August 24 as US secondary sanctions on Iran's oil exports and tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz materially constrained Middle East supply, before settling near approximately **$90/bbl** (approx., verify before merging) by month-end. WTI crude tracked near **$87/bbl** in late August. Surging diesel crack spreads, materially outpacing the headline crude move, pointed to tighter refined-product supply with direct implications for transportation, manufacturing, and agricultural cost inflation in key importing economies.

The commodity complex's August performance reinforces the thesis that supply-side geopolitical shocks — rather than demand-pull dynamics — are the dominant pricing mechanism in raw materials in the current cycle. For equities, the energy and metals rally materially boosted resource-sector earnings expectations. For central banks, it complicated the disinflation narrative at precisely the moment when headline CPI data had been approaching target, creating the difficult stagflationary undercurrent that framed Warsh's Jackson Hole remarks and will colour Q4 policy deliberations.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
US Treasuries were broadly range-bound through most of August before a sharp end-of-month repricing. The 10-year yield closed the month at **4.73%**, virtually unchanged from the July 31 level of **4.75%** — a **-2bps** move for the month that masked considerable intra-month volatility as competing forces largely offset one another. The 2-year yield, acutely sensitive to near-term Fed policy signals, jumped **+12bps** to **4.34%** on August 28 following Chair Warsh's Jackson Hole address, with fed funds futures repricing to embed a **60%** probability of a September rate hike.

Prior to Jackson Hole, the dominant fixed income narrative had been cautiously constructive: AI earnings strength, resilient economic data, and early signs of decelerating core inflation were collectively holding yields in a narrow range. Warsh's explicit acknowledgment that policy remains insufficiently restrictive abruptly ended this equilibrium, compressing the 2s10s spread (approx., verify before merging) and lifting short-end yields broadly across G10. German Bund and UK gilt yields rose in sympathy, as investors extrapolated a shared commitment among major central banks to maintaining restrictive policy in the face of energy-driven inflation persistence.

Fiscal dynamics remained a structural overhang throughout the month. The CBO's mid-month deficit projection update reignited the debate about Treasury supply sustainability at current yield levels, and the 10-year briefly exceeded **4.8%** in early September in the post-Warsh carry-through — suggesting the month-end hawkish shock has had material follow-through. For fixed income investors, August delivered a pointed lesson in duration asymmetry: gains accumulated over three weeks of stable yields were largely surrendered in the final two trading sessions, underscoring the binary risk embedded in holding duration against an uncertain Fed communication calendar.
